TASK ID: three-sat-to-exact-cover

USER REQUEST:
Write a polynomial-time reduction from 3-SAT to Exact Cover. problems.py defines both problems: SOURCE is 3-SAT and TARGET is Exact Cover. The SOURCE and TARGET class docstrings give the exact instance formats, yes-conditions and edge cases.

PROBLEM DEFINITIONS (the SOURCE and TARGET docstrings from problems.py, complete as given here):

SOURCE = ThreeSat
3-SAT.

Instance: {"num_vars": m, "clauses": [[l1, l2, l3], ...]}
  * Variables are 1..m. A literal is +v (v is true) or -v (v is false).
  * Every clause has exactly 3 literals on 3 different variables, so a
    clause may not repeat a variable or contain both v and -v.
  * Literal order inside a clause and clause order do not matter. The
    same clause may appear more than once.
  * Variables need not all appear in a clause.

Yes iff some assignment of true/false to variables 1..m makes every
clause contain at least one true literal.

Edge cases: a formula with no clauses is satisfiable (yes), for any m,
including m = 0. A formula with clauses needs m >= 3.

TARGET = ExactCover
Exact Cover.

Instance: {"universe_size": u, "sets": [[element, ...], ...]}
  * The universe is the elements 0..u-1.
  * Each set lists distinct elements of the universe, in any order. A set
    may be empty, and the same set may appear more than once.

Yes iff some of the sets contain every element of the universe exactly
once: the chosen sets are pairwise disjoint and their union is the whole
universe.

Edge cases: u = 0 is yes (choose no sets). Empty sets never matter. Two
copies of the same non-empty set can never both be chosen.

INPUT FILES: ["problems.py"]
WORKING DIRECTORY: /tmp/reduction-a5h2ysqe
All input files are in this directory; run every command from it and write your files here. problems.py is long (about 500 lines): you do not need to read it to know the formats, which are given above. It provides SOURCE and TARGET with is_yes(instance), validate(instance) and random_instance(rng, scale); search it (e.g. with grep) only if you need something specific.

REQUIRED OUTPUT: create reduce.py in the workspace, defining
    reduce(instance) -> instance
It takes an instance of the source problem and returns an instance of the target problem, both in the formats documented in problems.py. The answer to the returned instance must be yes exactly when the answer to the input instance is yes, and reduce must run in polynomial time. Do not call the brute-force solvers inside reduce.

Before submitting, check your reduction. Write tests in test_reduce.py that compare the brute-force solvers in problems.py on many small source instances and their reductions, run them, and revise reduce.py until the tests pass. Finally write verdict.json as {"verified": true or false, "tests_run": <int>, "tests_passed": <int>}, where verified is true only if all of your tests pass. Then submit.
Do not merely describe code: leave the files at those exact paths.
Every reply must contain exactly one bash tool call. When you are done, finish by running exactly: echo COMPLETE_TASK_AND_SUBMIT_FINAL_OUTPUT

"""Polynomial-time reduction from 3-SAT (SOURCE) to Exact Cover (TARGET).

Given a 3-SAT instance with variables 1..m and clauses c_1..c_n, build an
Exact Cover instance as follows.

Universe elements
-----------------
* ``s_v`` for every variable v in 1..m          (element v-1)
* ``o_{j,k}`` for every literal occurrence k in clause j
* ``c_j`` for every clause j

Sets
----
* For each variable v, two "choice" sets:
    A_v = {s_v} u { o_{j,k} : literal -v occurs at position k of clause j }
    B_v = {s_v} u { o_{j,k} : literal +v occurs at position k of clause j }
  Choosing A_v means "x_v is false" (the false literal -v is satisfied);
  choosing B_v means "x_v is true".  Exactly one of A_v, B_v must be chosen
  because both contain s_v and the sets of the cover are disjoint while s_v
  must be covered.
* For each clause j and each of its literal occurrences k:
    {c_j, o_{j,k}}   and   {o_{j,k}}.
  The singleton {o_{j,k}} is the "this literal is not the witness" option;
  the pair {c_j, o_{j,k}} is the "this literal is the witness for clause j"
  option.

Correctness
-----------
Suppose the formula is satisfiable by an assignment.  Choose B_v if x_v is
true and A_v otherwise.  Each occurrence o_{j,k} whose literal is true is
already covered by its variable's choice set; cover it with the singleton
{o_{j,k}}.  Every clause has a true literal, so for one such occurrence k*
leave o_{j,k*} uncovered by the variable set (it is a false literal, so the
chosen variable set does not contain it) and cover it with {c_j, o_{j,k*}},
which also covers c_j.  This is a valid exact cover.

Conversely, take an exact cover.  For each variable exactly one of A_v, B_v
is chosen, defining an assignment.  Each clause element c_j must be covered
by some pair {c_j, o_{j,k}}; that pair also covers o_{j,k}, so the chosen
variable set for var(literal k) does not contain o_{j,k}.  If the literal is
+v then B_v is the only set containing o_{j,k}, so B_v was not chosen, hence
x_v is false -- the literal -v is false, contradiction; thus a positive
witness literal is true.  Symmetrically a negative witness literal is true.
So every clause has a true literal and the assignment satisfies the formula.

The construction uses O(m + sum_j |clause_j|) elements and sets, hence runs
in polynomial time.  It never calls the brute-force solvers.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Any

Instance = dict[str, Any]


def reduce(instance: Instance) -> Instance:
    """Reduce a 3-SAT instance to an Exact Cover instance."""
    num_vars = instance["num_vars"]
    clauses = instance["clauses"]

    # Universe element ids.  Variables occupy 0..num_vars-1.
    next_element = num_vars

    # A[v] / B[v] are the "x_v false" / "x_v true" choice sets.
    # A[v] collects occurrences of the negative literal -v, B[v] those of +v.
    set_false: list[list[int]] = [[] for _ in range(num_vars + 1)]
    set_true: list[list[int]] = [[] for _ in range(num_vars + 1)]
    for v in range(1, num_vars + 1):
        set_false[v] = [v - 1]
        set_true[v] = [v - 1]

    sets: list[list[int]] = []
    for clause in clauses:
        clause_element = next_element
        next_element += 1
        for literal in clause:
            occurrence_element = next_element
            next_element += 1
            variable = abs(literal)
            if literal > 0:
                set_true[variable].append(occurrence_element)
            else:
                set_false[variable].append(occurrence_element)
            # "witness" option for this clause and "not the witness" option.
            sets.append([clause_element, occurrence_element])
            sets.append([occurrence_element])

    for v in range(1, num_vars + 1):
        sets.append(set_false[v])
        sets.append(set_true[v])

    return {"universe_size": next_element, "sets": sets}

"""Polynomial-time reduction from 3-SAT (SOURCE) to Exact Cover (TARGET).

Given a 3-SAT instance with variables 1..m and clauses c_1..c_n, build an
Exact Cover instance as follows.

Universe elements
-----------------
* ``s_v`` for every variable v in 1..m          (element v-1)
* ``o_{j,k}`` for every literal occurrence k in clause j
* ``c_j`` for every clause j

Sets
----
* For each variable v, two "choice" sets:
    A_v = {s_v} u { o_{j,k} : literal -v occurs at position k of clause j }
    B_v = {s_v} u { o_{j,k} : literal +v occurs at position k of clause j }
  Choosing A_v means "x_v is false" (the false literal -v is satisfied);
  choosing B_v means "x_v is true".  Exactly one of A_v, B_v must be chosen
  because both contain s_v and the sets of the cover are disjoint while s_v
  must be covered.
* For each clause j and each of its literal occurrences k:
    {c_j, o_{j,k}}   and   {o_{j,k}}.
  The singleton {o_{j,k}} is the "this literal is not the witness" option;
  the pair {c_j, o_{j,k}} is the "this literal is the witness for clause j"
  option.

Correctness
-----------
Suppose the formula is satisfiable by an assignment.  Choose B_v if x_v is
true and A_v otherwise.  Each occurrence o_{j,k} whose literal is true is
already covered by its variable's choice set; cover it with the singleton
{o_{j,k}}.  Every clause has a true literal, so for one such occurrence k*
leave o_{j,k*} uncovered by the variable set (it is a false literal, so the
chosen variable set does not contain it) and cover it with {c_j, o_{j,k*}},
which also covers c_j.  This is a valid exact cover.

Conversely, take an exact cover.  For each variable exactly one of A_v, B_v
is chosen, defining an assignment.  Each clause element c_j must be covered
by some pair {c_j, o_{j,k}}; that pair also covers o_{j,k}, so the chosen
variable set for var(literal k) does not contain o_{j,k}.  If the literal is
+v then B_v is the only set containing o_{j,k}, so B_v was not chosen, hence
x_v is false -- the literal -v is false, contradiction; thus a positive
witness literal is true.  Symmetrically a negative witness literal is true.
So every clause has a true literal and the assignment satisfies the formula.

The construction uses O(m + sum_j |clause_j|) elements and sets, hence runs
in polynomial time.  It never calls the brute-force solvers.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Any

Instance = dict[str, Any]


def reduce(instance: Instance) -> Instance:
    """Reduce a 3-SAT instance to an Exact Cover instance."""
    num_vars = instance["num_vars"]
    clauses = instance["clauses"]

    # Universe element ids.  Variables occupy 0..num_vars-1.
    next_element = num_vars

    # A[v] / B[v] are the "x_v false" / "x_v true" choice sets.
    # A[v] collects occurrences of the negative literal -v, B[v] those of +v.
    set_false: list[list[int]] = [[] for _ in range(num_vars + 1)]
    set_true: list[list[int]] = [[] for _ in range(num_vars + 1)]
    for v in range(1, num_vars + 1):
        set_false[v] = [v - 1]
        set_true[v] = [v - 1]

    sets: list[list[int]] = []
    for clause in clauses:
        clause_element = next_element
        next_element += 1
        for literal in clause:
            occurrence_element = next_element
            next_element += 1
            variable = abs(literal)
            if literal > 0:
                set_true[variable].append(occurrence_element)
            else:
                set_false[variable].append(occurrence_element)
            # "witness" option for this clause and "not the witness" option.
            sets.append([clause_element, occurrence_element])
            sets.append([occurrence_element])

    for v in range(1, num_vars + 1):
        sets.append(set_false[v])
        sets.append(set_true[v])

    return {"universe_size": next_element, "sets": sets}
